what_it_does: AI accelerator chips can run faster and cheaper if they skip (set to zero) some of the weight numbers in a neural network — a technique called structured sparsity — because the hardware can then skip those multiplications entirely. The most common approach, called N:M sparsity, forces exactly N non-zero values in every group of M weights in a single row, which is easy for hardware to exploit but causes the model to lose significant accuracy (over 6% worse on large language models at 50% sparsity) because it can only look at one dimension at a time. This paper introduces Transposable Block-wise Structured (TBS) sparsity, which finds a two-dimensional block pattern of zeros that works correctly whether the weight grid is read row-by-row or column-by-column — a property needed because neural network training reads weights in one direction and another pass reads them the other way. The matching hardware, TB-STC (a new design for the GPU-style math units that handle sparse math), includes an on-the-fly format converter and a smart scheduler that keeps the compute units fed, achieving about 1.5 times better memory bandwidth use and 1.6 times better compute efficiency.
